Welcome Humans: you are NOT the chosen one, rather you have been found to die in my game of death. Don't worry, you will most certainly die painfully while I laugh. So begins Despot Game, a weird cross between a RPG and turn-based battle simulator. You build armies, give them crazy weapons, line them up, and watch them get mowed down by robots, undead, mutant horrors, and our very own lord despot! All combat is automatic so placement and weapon options are key. This is a battle of resources: tokens to buy weapons and puny humans to restock losses, but will need some to boost passive buffs and feed your growing army (and starving humans are doomed). And once you loose all your humans you start again, though not completely new as new mutations and starter abilities unlock. The RPG elements come in two flavors: dungeon exploration to find the boss and exit, and random text events where you can gain or loose depending on your choices. All-in-all this game feels well made and similar to other death run games like Dead Cells or Hades, in this case its all about planning . . . and getting spammed by a necromancer 'cause your humans are too stupid to target him over the zombies!!

I made a list of some quality of life things I'd like to see in the full release:

- Better token signalling. It's hard to tell what gives tokens or how much. I would love to hear a token noise when monsters die or after a battle.
- More music variation, not just for battle, but switching into shops, bosses, curiosity rooms, etc
- Higher emphasis on sound effects. I had to turn down the music to even start hearing the sound effects, which weren't that punchy. For an idle battle game, I'd really love to hear some crunchy noises. There's no sound cues for many special abilities either, but when there are it makes a big difference.
- I wish we could see a keybinding list in the menu. I was wondering what hotkeys I was missing. (Like a cycle between human button?)
- I wish there was a better sense of objective. Are we trying to escape... kill the despot... is it endless? 
- More artistic chamber variation
- It's hard to tell enemy threat. With healthbars turned on, I wish enemies had a level to them.
- I wish clicking a text option had a sound effect.

Preferences:

- I wish some stats were divided by 10 or 5. I'd prefer a basic swordsman do 4.5 damage, rather than 45
- I wish leveling up healed humans
- I wish there was a scoring system to make dying in runs more fun. (New high score!)
- I wish there was an activated ability we could use -- like single use items we could buy.
- I think we get too many mutations. I would prefer starting with 2 slots for all the mutations we get, with more slots unlocked  with tokens. 
- I find tokens are a bit overused. I almost feel like there should be a third resource used for the research tree. 
- I wish WASD moved humans instead of switching chambers. I find using a mouse to reposition them somehow tedious
- I wish the humans were more active. I wish they would cheer after they win, or have conversation between them, or have a text box say "nooo!" when they die or something.
- I wish there was a better way to plan ahead, as part of the gameplay. Like, knowing you're facing a horde rather than a few tough robots would make you adjust your army a bit. As it is, since you don't know, the strategy feels independent of the game.

Почему в Деспотс Гейм стоит сыграть:
1. Шикарный пиксель арт и анимации (я как ярый фанат пикселей поставил арт на первое место, так как именно скриншоты и гифки "продали" мне эту игру)
2. Шикарный саундтрек. Почти не надоедает, есть несколько любимых треков, которые я жду постоянно. Как я понял музыка на рейд выбирается случайным образом.
3. Интересная идея. Мы видели много рогаликов, очень много рогаликов. Я не могу сказать, что Деспотс Гейм лучший из них, но он определённо выделяется из общей кучи. Механика автобоя может стать для кого-то минусом, но составлять отряды из различных бойцов, которые комбинируются между собой - затягивает. И после проигрыша всегда хочется сразу же попробовать забежать в подземелье снова, но уже с другим сетапом.
4. Мультиплейер. Пока что он где-то далеко за 10+ этажом (не знаю сколько их точно), но в демке это была довольно забавная активность, которая так же заставляла пробежать подземелье ещё и ещё, даже если оно проходилось с закрытыми глазами.

Возможно игра не понравится тем фанатам рогаликов, которые любят оттачивать ловкость своих рук на геймпадах, потому что тут скил пальцев и реакции вообще ничего не решает. Придётся прокачивать знание игры, классов, их умений и где-то даже браться за калькулятор, высчитывая какого количество маны будет достаточно для твоего отряда и кого будет выгоднее купить здесь и сейчас. Умение всё это делать приходит не сразу, и если продолжать в тупую бегать по подземелью, пройти хоть сколько-нибудь далеко не получится. 

Как итог: Любишь пиксельные игры? Любишь рогалики, где каждая ошибка может стереть весь твой прогресс? Любишь разбираться в статах, абилках и комбинациях разных юнитов? Тогда, эта игра для тебя.

[h1] I [strike]wanted to[/strike] love this game [/h1]

An auto-battler with an ungodly amount of pop-culture references? An awesome art style with fantastic animations? "Sign me up!"

[b]The Expectations[/b]

Game fun character cool

[strike]This game sets itself up with the mechanics of the auto-battlers we've come to love. Relax, and grab things from different factions to build into powerful bonuses, then soup that up further with the extra abilities/modifiers (in this game called mutations) you pick up along the way. A tried-and-true formula at this point! You can even face other players once you've beaten the game, bringing in that competitive element we all love. This all falls apart once you've touched your first playthrough.[/strike]

[b]The Game[/b]

Gameplay nice quite fun very upgrade

[strike]The gameplay loop you'll be put through goes as follows: pick a starting team, walk room to room fighting enemies, and use the tokens you obtain to buy stronger items and strengthen your generic mutations, all while balancing your resources. Not too dissimilar from auto-battlers like Dota Underlords or SnakeRX! But then you start to notice that it IS quite different than those you've played before - and not in a good way. 

Gone are the fun, varied builds, as you're railroaded to putting disposable tanks in the front and forced to focus on upgrading HP and attack speed in the generic mutation tree, so that your team doesn't fall behind. Gone are the fun different abilities amidst the different factions. Excited to see how this level 3 mage item might differ from the level 1 item? That's the baffling part - it doesn't! It only changes the visuals. No matter the item your puny human might be holding, he has the exact same abilities as his other mages or fighters - just an auto-attack. No interesting ability, no variation, just a DIRECT stats upgrade from the previous levels. As well, the only way to level up that boring, singular faction ability is to hold on to weak, inferior, and unupgradable units. This is in no way interesting and is at odds with itself mechanically. I must constantly buy the most expensive item to survive, and yet keep throwing men to the wolves with crappy level 1 and 2 items so that my team even has synergy? You can't combine level 1 items, you can't improve the base guys you put them on, they are simply pure fodder and tedium. The absolute inability for my characters to have relevance outside of my level 4 and 5 characters is ridiculous to me. It's disheartening to want to try out the 5/5 faction bonus, because I know I'll have the slog of bringing along some useless level 1 items to do it.  You don't even get to see a different ability - this character on your team is just an inferior version of something else you have. And even if I give them the benefit of the doubt, that you're supposed to have this revolving door of useless low-level item users that can't survive long enough to level up, when they die in accordance to the gameplay loop the developers designed, you are beholden to a coin flip on whether or not you can even reuse that item or if it disappears into the void for you to have to purchase again for yourself. To design a puzzle, then limit it via coin-flip, is frankly a lazy attempt to get folk to put in more hours due to runs that flat out fail.

Gone is the experimentation, as one simple click can cost you tons of food resources, as the game penalises you for backtracking, and even for simply walking through empty rooms. An odd, tax-like food system exists in this game seemingly only to stop you from backtracking. With multiple ways to spend your currency already, you are forced to drop some on food that your people munch down on in every room - empty or not. Better have lucked out and gone the right way initially, because every empty room your people walk through is as exhausting for them as a battle to the death.

Last, when you're in the midst of having fun, and you're finally at the fight where you die, what is it you want after? Feedback. You want to understand the mechanics of where you died and how to improve, and that's the final place where this game falls flat. There is ZERO feedback. Zero information as to why you are losing - unless it's obvious like the manhacks on the first level that will kill two of your melee units regardless of your choices when you're playing Normal>Classic. You will be soaring, and then you will have to watch your entire team die, or at least dwindle over a few fights, with nothing you can do. Uninteractive, artificially difficult gameplay. You have no player agency when you die, you have nothing to outplay amidst watching them die, no skill to rely on, no meta upgrades to get to improve your next run, you just lose because the game gave you a random stat check you couldn't pass. Yes, I could pick different starting loadouts or lower the difficulty, but that won't give me anymore information as to why the initial team they give is set up to fail against a possible first fight.

And what is the solution to the gripes as seen in the reviews? Focus on health and attack speed upgrades in the generic tree, constantly buy the highest-level items available, put disposable tanks up front, and play on other game modes as apparently the normal mode isn't balanced. These are not proper solutions. If you HAVE to choose an option, then it is no longer an option but a required tax, and there's a good amount of those in this game. To succeed you will have to do similar builds over and over, with little to no variation between your runs as you attempt to find the best ranged items to hide behind your fodder after you realise there's no point to experimenting with faction bonuses.

It's good to shake up the formula, and it's good to question the practices of the auto-battlers of yore to see what they can change and make different, but frankly the changes here do not make for a better game.[/strike]

I would love to re-do this whole thing one day, but I'll sum it up as 'they made this game even better'. These devs are top notch.

5.5/10 - A fascinating, deep and utterly insane game that somehow feels like it doesn't want you to play it. A very cautious recommendation. Full  review below.

= Intro =

Had my eye on this for a while, as I enjoy autobattlers and the sheer scale of the fights (and bonkers units) in this immediately caught my interest.

= Gameplay: 5/10 =

Where do I even start with this one?

It's basically Binding of Isaac, crossed with an autobattler (you control unit selection and positioning, and combat plays out automatically). You buy and equip humans with weapons and gear, ranging from shields, swords and magic rings to laser rifles and tesla coils, to tables, ping-pong paddles and footballs (wat) and then move from room to room, 'clearing' each one of enemies. 

'Wat' is very much the mood this game seems to be going for. Despot's Game has a serious case of the galloping crazies. Not only are the references and memes omnipresent, but the loadouts, enemies and dialogue are all just...weird. It feels like it's trying to be Undertale, sometimes - not a bad thing, but it occasionally comes over as forced (but mostly entertaining).

It all feels pretty good, especially once you get a veritable army of dudes flinging spells, heals, lasers and slashes around. 

However, the game is held back by a few odd design decisions.

The 'food' system is the biggie for me - every time you change rooms (including rooms you've already cleared) you lose food, proportional to the size of your army. Food, however, is not exactly common and you burn through so much of it so fast that it's easy for a bad run of luck, or a single wrong turn in some maps to set you up for a slow, irreversible defeat. Maybe it's a 'git gud' thing and I simply don't understand how it's meant to operate, but honestly, this system could be completely removed and, to me, the game would feel all the better for it.

The difficulty also feels deliberately spiteful, and with the sheer randomness involved combined with the 'hands off' nature of autobattlers...yeah. RNG frustration, even by the standards of roguelikes. It's screaming out for some sort of persistent skill-tree or levelling system to make future runs easier, obviously disabled for the multiplayer 'King of the Hill' leaderboard mode.

The game is incredibly deep, with oodles of different weapons, enemies, bosses, unit combos, systems and the like - and it'll take a while to get a grasp on it, especially with how little information is provided. I'm still not entirely sure what 90% of the weapons actually really do, let alone which ones to pick.

It's all a mess. A fun mess, sure, but still a mess. It's hard to tell what is deliberate and what is just a part of a rough-around-the-edges Early Access game.

= Graphics and Audio: 6.5/10 =

The game has a simple pixel-art style that works...okay. Designs are simple, but distinct. It does start looking really monotone before too long though, thanks to the palette. I'll be dreaming in purple and blue tonight. Maybe it becomes more varied later on?

The music is rather grating, and I turned it off after a few minutes. This is definitely the sort of game to bash out while watching a podcast.

= Value: 7/10 =

There is a lot of variety and depth here, especially for the pretty reasonable asking price. However, this all depends on your tolerance for frustration and willingness to bash your head against a wall until you understand what's going on and all the systems click. 

It does appear that this game is still pretty early-on in development, so it'll be interesting to see how it grows and improves in the coming months.

= Overall =

+ Original
+ Deeper than most autobattlers out there
+ Some references are fun, and often quite obscure
+ Some cool and creative unit/monster designs

- Overwhelmingly complex
- Food system is anti-fun
- Frustratingly RNG, even by roguelike standards
- Badly needs some sort of 'between game' progression, if difficulty will remain as is
- 'Quirkiness' can feel forced at times

At the end of the day, I have no idea how to feel about this - there is so much to like here, and yet so much that pushes me away. I have to tip my hat at the 'this is my game, and I'm making it the way I want' auteur developer (reminds me of the nearly perfect Gemcraft series in that regard). However, doing this runs the risk of alienating potential players, and making your game incredibly niche. 

As things stand, I both am glad that I bought this - and yet just don't feel the urge to play it more right now. Still, if it appeals to you, the price is definitely right. If you are on the fence...maybe wait and see how it develops.

[h1] If you're into tactical roguelikes and want to experience the best strategy game of 2021, you should buy Despot's Game. [/h1]

[b]A Run[/b]

A run consists of several levels where each level has a few rooms and each room has an enemy to fight until the boss fight at the end. You will receive money after every room you fight in, this is where the strategy comes in and you have to plan ahead as you need the money to buy humans, food, class items, and mutations.

Some room have mutation altars where you get a free mutation to help you through your run & some rooms have random events which requires you to do a small quest and then rewards you with something awesome. Once you’ve beaten the level boss you will proceed to the next level and another random event will happen which will help you in the upcoming level.

[b]Battles[/b]

The battles are quite easy to understand…

You have puny humans, either newbies or with a class item attached. You can place the puny humans in the room however you want, once you’re satisfied with where your humans are you can click on "Fight" and the battle begins. from here on, it’s an auto-battler. Your humans will automatically fight, and you can sit back and watch and hope that your puny humans kick ass in the room.

[b]Humans[/b]

Humans are your main resource. Each human needs one food for every room they go into. If you don't have enough food left, you will suffer from debuffs and then your humans will die. Some rooms allow you to buy food with money but if you don’t have money or you can’t get to one of these rooms you can sacrifice one human for five pieces of food.

[b]Classes[/b]

Every human starts of naked or as they call it a newbie, the newbies will then have to be equipped with a class item to increase their stats & help your army grow stronger. There are a lot of different classes available like Tanks, Shooter, Medics, Fighters, Cultist, Wizards, Ninjas and so many more.

As of now you have 5 different weapons in one class.

Having humans equipped with a different weapon in one class grants them special abilities, for example having three cultists with different weapons will let them summon tentacles from the ground which will help you in battle & having 3 tanks with different class items will taunt the enemy to ensure they fight the tanks first. This also adds to the tactical depth of the game.

[b]King of the Hill[/b]

King of the hill is the multiplayer part of the game. it’s very thrilling even though you sit back and watch your army kick other real world people’s army’s asses. Once you’ve won a round on the normal mode or higher your army will be placed in the leader board, from here on you will battle against other players army one by one. If you beat the army you will move up the ‘King of the Hill” ladder essentially taking their spot on the leader board & if you lose you will move down.

[b]Overall Progression[/b]

Currently there isn’t anything to make your future runs easier or different from the previous run except for the procedural generation & unlocking different play modes & starting builds but this doesn’t enhance gameplay or add any mutations from the previous run you’ve had.

[b]Cons[/b]

I don’t know if I must just “Get Good”, but the early access is quite difficult compared to the demo which could have been too easy. I am a few hours into the game without stopping and I haven’t reached the end boss very often. In these hours I have done countless runs and came across similar events after about 3 runs. This made it quite monotones and easier as I knew exactly what to answer to get the bonus mutation or money.

[b]Pros[/b]

The pros definitely outweighs the cons, Despot’s Game is tactically demanding as there is a lot of strategy involved to win a run and be placed in the leader board.

You will have a lot of internal debate in where to place your humans, what class items you need to buy for your newbies & if you have enough food to last you a few more rooms until you reach another room where you can buy some.

The money management plays a major role in the strategy of the game which makes is very fun.

There is some kind of RNG that doesn’t feel unfear the room layouts, random events in the levels, selection of class items, mutations & enemy spawns feel quite balanced and it won’t make you feel cheated rather It made me feel like I should have made smarter decisions instead of blaming the RNG.

I am not a big fan of leader board aspects in games, but the King of the Hill leader board element is surprisingly fun. It’s hilarious to see your army in the leader board and how it kicks other army’s asses without you barely lifting a finger.

The random events writing is amazing, funny and very creative with a lot of references which will put a smile on your face.

[b]Conclusion[/b]

In Conclusion Despot’s Game is a very addictive, tactical demanding, humours, innovative and fun game which will keep you busy for hours at end. I can’t get enough of this game; I do enjoy the optimisation of the RNG & the different root the developers took with the leader board and the King of the Hill mechanic. This early in the early access the game feels quite polished, but needs more meat to for example more events, more mutation, improving yourself with each run & definitely a wider range of enemies and bosses.

[i]Despot’s Game: Dystopian Army Builder is one of the best strategy games I’ve played in 2021 and in my opinion, it deserves to be in the list for best strategy games of 2021[/i]

[h1] Its a difficult recommendation [/h1]
[b] Let me explain:[/b]

[i]The Good Stuff[/i]
- The core gameplay is fun and you really switch positions around and try to have weapons of any tier equipped
- Plenty of Mutations unlockable 
- Different Starts with different Loadouts 
- Most balanced Food mechanic I have seen so far. It is important to keep your guys fed but you dont have to run from food store to food store.
- Balancing Act between overall Upgrades, A bigger and better Force and Food is well worth some "i`d rather have money" decisions
- Mini Quests with cute little references for a bit of diversity

[i]The Meh or plain Bad Stuff[/i]
- Weapon Variety seems Lack Luster. You will see them all really damn quickly.
- There is a good amount of Classes or Categories rather, but not all of them are viable. Eggheads and Fighters seem really bad overall, Tanks are only good early game, while Medics, Cultists and Tricksters carry you hard.
- The balance just isn't there. Everytime you build up a powerful force and think to yourself "I finally do it this time" you will be killed by the next floor. This happens especially often in the Green Zone, where Everything has AOE, deletes your Armor, Stuns you for 3 Seconds whilst the Ability itself has a 5 second Cooldown and overall anything jumps to wherever your healers and shooters are. In the Middle? They jump in the middle. Backline? Oh look, the entire Room is behind your Frontline. In the Frontline? They just go straight ahead.
- Once your healers are out of mana or you get one or two wiped, it is most likely game over. You will not recover, even if you manage to beat that room. You cannot recover. Once you are past the First two stages you either win or lose on a room to room basis. If the Boss, like the Cerberus for example, AOE hits your entire Party with his paws, while his minions reduce your armor by 999, you just loose. He two to threeshots 20 People at once. And since this is an Auto-Chess game, good luck seeing the fun in that.
- Target prioritisation is off. Your Dudes attack whats closest. You cannot set priorities or influence them in any other way, other than placing them there. Your Healers will heal the next person, even if he hasnt gotten damaged yet. Your Tanks will all run down whilst your squishy shooters run up and get absolutely destroyed.

Overall I had my fun with it and probably will try to beat it every other time I find myself on the train but there is much to do here and it is far from an experience I can 100% recommend.

[h1]Despot’s Game: Dystopian Army Builder - B-[/h1]

[b][u]Who This Game is For:[/u][/b]
Those who enjoy challenging roguelike games or have a personal vendetta against the human race. Think “Binding of Isaac” but you build and manage an army. 

[table]
    [tr][th][url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/37839913/]Click Me to Follow My Curator Page for more reviews![/url][/th][/tr]

[b][u]Summary:[/u][/b]
Despot’s Game is a roguelike army building simulator. The goal here is to build your army through buying Humans and equipping them with weapons. You go from room to room, while managing your food, and fighting a wave of enemies until you beat the Boss room and go to the next level. Beating each room gives you tokens and either a weapons shop, to buy weapons and more humans, a random ability/mutation, or absolutely nothing. You can also manage unit placement on the map and then watch your army fight and level up. Getting further in a run will unlock new abilities/mutations. The core gameplay loop is solid, enjoyable, and unique. The game has pixel graphics, but I believe the art is quite well made and really works with maintaining the dystopian theme. I am conflicted though. On one hand, I love these kinds of games. On the other hand, it feels this game’s mechanics sometimes hinder your progression in the game. For example, getting abilities for your classes come in 1 of 2 ways: You can either get it randomly from a drop or have at least 2-3 people in the same class but with different weapons equipped. I feel this is detrimental to the game and got me to stop caring about abilities and just get the strongest equipment. I believe this game has a lot of potential, but the mechanics working against the player are too strong. I see a lot of potential and did enjoy my time playing, but there are some issues that I believe really need to be worked out.

[i]Disclaimer: The game was played on my main account, so this doesn't have my accurate in-game time.[/i]

[b][u]BREAKDOWN (Grading Key at the bottom):[/u][/b]

[b][u]Graphics – A-:[/u][/b]
The game is styled with pixel-art, which does a great job evoking the dystopian setting. Not all the art is made with excruciating detail, but there is enough to keep the theme alive and varied. Different levels have different themes, which are reflected in the rooms. Each room on one level sticks within that theme with small changes like slightly different walls or graffiti on the floor. Since it is dystopian, the setting is dark, which is something I personally like, because too many bright colors hurt my eyes. The humans have a pink, simple design which changes with their class. Some of these classes are more visually pleasing than others, like the One Punch Man equipment.  My favorite design aspect of this game is the enemies. Each enemy looks unique and creative. From Cabbage monsters to robot samurai, the game has a variety of enemies with great designs. The animations of the attacks aren’t top tier, but it felt fluid enough to enjoy watching the battles. All in all, the setting is great, animations are fluid, and designs are creative and varied.

[b][u]Gameplay – C+:[/u][/b]
The gameplay is where I get very conflicted. The game is positioned to be a roguelike-management game. You start the game by choosing a difficulty and starting crew, both of which are unlocked by playing the game and performing different actions or having a specific team setup. From there, you position your humans and start clearing out rooms while getting tokens, new weapons, or a random mutation/ability. You also must manage how much food you have. When you go to a new room, you will consume 1 food per 1 human on the field. So, if you have a team of 15 humans, they will consume 15 food every time they go into a room, including ones you have already cleared out. To get more food, you must either find a food shop room or sacrifice some humans you must get food.  When a boss is killed, you will go to the next level and prompt an event to get tokens, new people, or abilities that make your team worse. The weapons/class system is my biggest gripe. Buying weapons and equipping them to your humans gives them a class. Each class is unique in how it’ll fight, whether it be a tank with lots of HP and defense or a shooter which attacks from afar. There are many different classes that are diverse in how they play. Each one has multiple different weapons within that class that range from common to very rare. All classes have abilities, but 90% of them are only active when you have 2-3 members of the same class but with different weapons from that class. So if you have 2 people who have the same weapon, the ability won’t be active. Abilities can also be upgraded if you have more than 3 people to a class with different weapons. On top of that, getting the different weapons for the classes can be a slog. You can upgrade the shop to show more than 4 weapons, but with so many classes, it can be difficult to find the ones you need. I’ve also realized some of the abilities can range from great to useless. For example, the tank ability, which taunts enemies to attack them and increases their defense by 50% or more, is a wonderful ability. On the other side of the spectrum, the Tricksters ability allows each Trickster to throw a bomb that deals 30 damage AoE. While this may seem good, you’ll be fighting enemies with 1000+ health, so its ultimately worthless. Even healers, who don’t need any requirement to be able to use their healing ability, only heal 15 damage pre-upgrade. Enemies do 50+ damage after the first level, so it is also useless. The humans can also be killed during battles which could make you lose your abilities you worked so hard to get. You may be able to recover the weapon and just put it on a new human you buy, but that is not guaranteed. It is a frustrating system that needs some polish for sure. 

[b][u]Replayability B-:[/u][/b]
This is a roguelike game, so replayability is at its core. Every time you die, you unlock new abilities you can get. If you complete certain actions or have specific team class setups before you die, you can unlock new starting lineups and difficulties. The difficulties and starting lineups are unique and offer different ways to start the game, even though you’ll end up going for whatever hits hardest in the end. There is also a King of the Hill mode where you fight against other players. This mode does have seasons to it with winners of each season. As of right now, I would say there is enough replayability to keep me hooked for 20-25 hours. I can see this changing depending on future updates, and they seem to have a good roadmap for the future.

[b][u]Multiplayer C+:[/u][/b]
This game has something called asynchronous multiplayer. Basically, you can fight against other teams that have survived the main game. It will not be controlled in real-time by another player; it is something they have set up and let you challenge them. This is the King of the Hill mode. It seems the devs have a new mode with a focus on multiplayer coming, but it has not been implemented yet, so don’t go into this game hoping for an engaging multiplayer mode, at least not yet.

[b][u]Developers B+:[/u][/b]
At the time of this review, the dev has released two updates to the game since its early access release one month ago, culminating in new enemies, mutations, and balancing, with some little hotfixes pushed in the middle. They seem to be pushing their King of the Hill mode and community interaction and involvement when it comes to development, which sounds wonderful. If they continue this streak, I will put faith in their support. I have read a couple of developer comments to negative reviews and I was happy with their responses. They were appreciative of the review, open to criticism, and willing to discuss problems and how to fix them. TinyBuild is also publishing the game, which gives me faith the game won't be abandoned.

After only 3 hours with the game I have to say it's by far one of the best Rogue-lite experiences I've ever had.

The rogue-lite genre is a personal favourite of mine and this game has peaked my interest for awhile now so I decided to give it a try. I'm typically not into games where I am not in total control of things, but this game changed that. 

SPOILERS AHEAD FOR MANY THINGS IN THE GAME! YOU HAVE BEEN WARNED!

The gameplay is very simple yet has a deeper level of strategy to it almost like a game of chess. You can individually move your puny humans around wherever you'd like. This can decide which of your puny humans takes the enemy aggression first. You can "customize" (I use that word loosely) your puny humans with different items you buy in the shops that pop up in certain rooms. Want a team full of ranged attackers? Buy guns and magic. Want a super tanky team that just goes balls deep? Buy shields and swords. The choice is completely up to the player on how they want to play out their battles.

You also need to keep in mind your characters "hunger" and the size of your party. You have a set amount of food you start with. Each room you move to take 1 food per puny human in your party. Running out of food and moving reduced your parties combat effectiveness more and more the more you move without eating. This mechanic is very interesting and something to always be keeping in mind.

I personally fell in love with the game as soon as I finished my first level. Once you dive deeper into the maze you are greeted with a short "ZORK" like text adventure. This can have many different outcomes. Some beneficial like free tokens or characters, and some not so beneficial like having a party member lose HP or even flat out die at random. Some of these texts have easter eggs in them (easter eggs are EVERYWHERE in this game I love it so much. Well done devs, well done.). One of which prompted me meeting a "Blue Ninja" who forgot how to shoot ice. I then had to select the proper text prompts to remind him for the reward of a magic ring for one of my puny humans. (Sub-Zero easter egg? YES PLEASE! Thank god I knew how to throw his ice orb....but do you know?)

There are tons of hilarious side encounters to have as well with chance NPC's. One of which is a hole that will eat "newbies" and give you a reward. Another being a scientist generating power by having a zombie scare a newbie on a treadmill. They had a lot of fun making this game and I can't wait to see what else comes in the future.

There is still a lot for me to see with this game and I can't wait to dive deeper. The game never takes itself to seriously so you can just play it to kill time with some music on in the background as I do. Very fun experience overall.

I haven't bumped into issues at all in my time playing, nor have I any complaints. I do however wish there was a mechanic that allowed you to prioritize targets in combat. I found myself in the later stages dying due to my puny humans fighting the wrong target and getting mauled to death by a much more dangerous foe. You do have the freedom to rearrange your puny humans before combat but if the biggest threat spawns behind others you don't have a way of prioritizing that threat.

With all that said for a Rogue-lite this game is completely unique in design from anything I've ever played. I'd like to give it a score out of 10.

Despot's Game: Dystopian Army Builder is another solid game published by Tinybuild, and developed by Konfa Games who also made Despotism 3k.

In this game you command an army of puny red humans and go from room to room and biome to biome fighting groups of enemies like robots and mutants. As you clear rooms, you earn tokens to buy more humans to replace fallen ones, as well as mutations, weapons, and whatnot. There are also some management parts like your humans needing food sustenance to perform and fight to their optimal ability. As you move around rooms the amount of food is consumed, so more is required to be bought with the tokens earned. Also, more troops mean more food being consumed, and fewer troops mean less fighting power. So, managing your army and tokens is a key part of the game. More people and equipment can be bought and assigned to, like buy a few troops and some shields, rings, and swords etc. The fighting sequences are fun to watch as you arrange them in certain orders manually or have them auto-assigned. When you play the fight button, watch as they charge and fight the enemies which is quite satisfying. Overall, it is quite a tactical game as build your army and fight hordes of enemies.

The pixel art visuals are great to look at as someone who loves pixel art, with colour palette being used well with the dark kind of tone for the background and characters. The vast array of enemies does also keep the game fresh, and it is fun to watch them being taken down. The teeny red humans themselves are cute to observe, especially when there are plenty of them and when the screen is zoomed in for a closer view. Music is another solid point with catchy robotic and groovy tunes playing as you play the game.

Price of the game is rather fair for what it has to offer. It can easily be played for hours are there are several difficulties and classes to choose from when unlocked. Having played it so far, it has been a smooth and fun experience so that is another positive. The game is currently in early access and more content will be added to improve the game throughout the phase. Overall, it is a very enjoyable roguelike game that is most definitely worth taking note of.

Despot's Game: Dystopian Army Builder
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Despot’s Game is a fun little roguelike, tactical, strategy game. There’s a lot of roguelike strategy games out there, and some are really good and some not so much. 

But there’s nothing quite like Despot’s Game! Developed by Konfa Games, Despot’s Game takes you on a wild adventure of miniaturized army-building and combat, with some of the wackiest and fun concepts I have come across in a while. 

You play as the brain of the mission and get to take control of an army of oddly dressed nut jobs with baguettes as weapons! 

Gameplay: The game goes about its mission in runs; each run consists of levels and each room consists of a few enemies to a large group of enemies or some big ones until the boss fights at the end. 

This is where the strategy part kicks in, starting with a few almost naked troops and bare minimum weapons. As you see your troops get smashed into bits you realize, ya it's about time I should start getting more weapons and troops. 

To move further into the game you need more troops, weapons, clothes, and mutations, and for that you need money. But lucky for you some rooms come with free mutation alters and there are quite a few events/quests here and there, so those too will help as well.

Combat: The combat is super simple here, at the beginning of every round you place your troops as you like; I recommend going with the tanks first and ranged weapons second, and then the rest will follow. 

When you think you are satisfied with your troop placement, just hit fight and the combat begins. 

It’s all automated, so you just sit back and pray that your placement was okay and that you win. 

Humans:  Good old flesh and blood puny humans! Yah this is your most important resource. To maintain your army, each human requires one food item in each room they go into, and if you run out of food, no worries just make them eat one of their own. 

But that won’t be the case if you have money on you, and you walk into rooms from where you can buy food.

Class system: You start off with naked troops called newbies and as you gain enough money you will have to equip them with class-based items. This makes your army stronger, and you get unique classes of troops like Tanks, Medics, Shooters, Cultists, Wizards, Ninjas, and more. 

There is also this fun system called clause, where if you equip your troops with three of the same weapon, you get added buffs and abilities. 

And there is also a multiplayer element with a leaderboard system, but sadly it didn’t work out for me. 

World design: Despot’s Game has this fun rusty, wet, pixel graphic feel to it, which may not sound appetizing for some, but trust me, it’s a charm to look at. 

As the game progresses through tight rooms, vents, and small outdoor areas, you get to appreciate the effort that went into the game’s development. 

Positives: 

+ Fun casual roguelike experience 
+ Sit back and watch the carnage. 
+ Mini quests 
+ Tactically demanding 
+ Importance of money management 
+ Fun and unique items 

Negatives: 

- No negatives 

A fun tactical game, where you can just sit back, relax and watch the carnage unfold as your puny humans go on a rampage. 

8/10

 Another major issue is once you're losing, runs are almost always over with no hopes of coming back. To gain strength, you need to go to a shop room, to gain access to the shop, you need to beat the enemies in the room. So if you're weak, or you just got half your squad wiped, it's almost impossible to recover since to regain your manpower you need to be strong in the first place.

In conclusion, the core gameplay loop is great, and because it is still in early access I am hopeful that they will polish the gameplay some more.

Despot's Game is not an optimal game.

It's got a good gameplay loop, but that same loop intrudes on the roguelike mechanics instead of enhancing them. Permadeath is an intended feature, but the story doesn't recognize it - you may exhaust a lot of the dialogue choices available early on, only to see them reused on your 3rd run. The levels are short, but can also end you quickly if you aren't lucky or careful enough.

I can come up with dozens of mechanical critiques for the game, but they don't actually make it any less fun. And that's because DG's core experience is good.

The writing is charming. The setting is surprisingly unique. There's a lot of enemy variety and playstyle options, and the roguelite elements make it easy to make progress after a failed run.

It *does* feel a little bare considering it's in early access, but even so, Despot's Game feels special. Like the player, it's making mistakes. It's learning. It's improving as it grows.

I'd recommend it with very few reservations, and I'm eager to see what the devs do next.

Quick Description:
-Despot's Game is a dungeon crawling autobattler w/ charm and intrigue for days.  This game is the perfect mix of challenge, mystery, full on weirdness, and a good shake of tactics.  The learning curve is quite steep, but this is one of the very best autobattlers out there.  There is a ton of content already, less than a year into early access, and I am really excited to see what gets added by the 1.0 release.

What's Good:
-I love how strategic this game is.  You will need to decide which room to enter in the dungeon, how to position your units, which upgrades to purchase, when to buy new types of units, and when to buy more food to keep your army at full strength.  This is exactly what I was hoping for from an autobattler.  When you are successful, it is b/c you have made good decisions, which makes this game feel really tactical.  
-I am a huge fan of the visual style!  The pixel art is detailed, really cool visually, and I love all of the different types of army units, monsters, and terrifying bosses.  I love the blend between robots and monsters, and it works really well here.  
-The skill ceiling is extremely high in this game.  This game will kick your ass until you start to adapt.  When I play this game, it kind of feels like if Enter the Gungeon were an autobattler and had really bizarre robot monsters.  I have played for almost 7 hrs, and I still have so much more to learn on my way to having a victorious run.
-There is a good amount of build variety during runs.  The devs keep adding more content which is great, but as of now, there is still a ton of unique and really cool synergies.  Putting together the perfect army that is balanced is such a great feeling.  I love being able to steamroll a group of baddies in the dungeon when my army starts to become powerful.

Could Use Some Changes:
-Hopefully, by the 1.0 release, the devs will add a more detailed tutorial.  This is fairly complex game.  I didn't even realize for the first few hrs that I could manually upgrade my units in a skill tree.  This is something that should be covered in a tutorial.  
-I would also like to see more variety in enemy types, alternative bosses, and dungeon variety.  The more variety you have, the better.  It's challenging for the devs, b/c everything must be balanced, but it would help make runs more unique and keep players coming back for more.  It would be great if there were alternative dungeons that you could visit or potentially alternative paths that you can select from, just a thought.
-As I mentioned earlier, every roguelight in early access needs more items, more synergies, and more meta progression.  This game is no exception.  It seems to be lacking quite a bit in meta progression, so that's an area I'm hoping they focus on in the future.  I'm really excited to see how this game shapes up over the next 6-12 months.

Consensus:
-Solid Game (Tier 3 and makes up 35% of my reviews).  This looks like the quintessential autobattler, but really shines in artistic direction, really unique army balance, and really high fun factor.  I wasn't the biggest fan of this genre before this game, but I'm now a believer.  I'm really excited to explore this genre more and see how this gem turns out once it reaches it's 1.0 release.

Despot’s Game: Dystopian Battle Simulator, developed by Konfa Games and published by tinyBuild, is a wonderfully chaotic blend of roguelike structure, auto-battler mechanics, and dark satire. It throws players into the role of an unseen overseer commanding an army of naked, amnesiac humans through a procedurally generated maze full of deadly traps, strange enemies, and absurd upgrades. The game manages to stand out in a crowded indie field by embracing a unique tone—equal parts dystopian sci-fi and self-aware absurdity—while challenging players to survive, strategize, and adapt in a constantly shifting environment.

The core gameplay revolves around recruiting units, equipping them with bizarre weapons, and organizing them into formations that will do battle automatically. This auto-battling is the heart of the experience—once a battle begins, the player's role is reduced to that of a spectator, watching as their decisions on army composition and positioning play out in real time. The satisfaction comes from seeing synergy between units come to life, especially as classes start to evolve through the accumulation of specific weapons. Whether you’re building a team of laser gunners, vampire mages, cultists with tentacles, or fencers wielding literal pretzels, the joy comes from experimentation and discovering which combinations work best—or hilariously fail.

Every decision matters. Movement through the dungeon consumes food, which is a critical resource. Run out, and your squad becomes weakened and demoralized. In extreme cases, starvation can lead to in-fighting and the death of your units, adding a survival layer to the strategic loop. This mechanic forces players to consider the risks of exploring every room versus rushing to the exit. Shops, event rooms, and elite battles each offer potential rewards, but also introduce a degree of randomness that can make or break a run. Sometimes you find powerful synergies or class upgrades that transform your build into a steamrolling machine; other times, you're stuck with gear that has no meaningful synergy and a group of meatbags doomed to die in a corner of the dungeon.

Visually, the game embraces a clean, vibrant pixel-art style. Characters and environments are easy to read, despite the growing chaos of battle as units stack up, cast spells, and unleash devastating attacks. The humor embedded in the art—units wearing plungers on their heads, firing sausages from cannons, or summoning lightning bolts from giant anime swords—keeps the mood light despite the oppressive sci-fi backdrop. Complementing this is a pulsing, synth-heavy soundtrack that reinforces the game’s dystopian tone while maintaining a sense of fun. The aesthetic choices echo the game’s writing, which leans heavily into irreverence, breaking the fourth wall and often mocking the player or the absurd situation they’re in.

There is a multiplayer layer that adds an interesting endgame twist: once players complete the dungeon, their squad is pitted against those of other players in asynchronous PvP battles. This adds an element of competition and long-term planning, encouraging players to think not just about surviving the dungeon, but also building a team strong enough to survive endgame duels. The competitive meta is surprisingly deep, and watching your units compete against others’ optimized builds brings a satisfying payoff to each run—especially when it ends in victory.

That said, Despot’s Game isn’t without its flaws. One of the most consistent criticisms is the degree to which randomness can dictate success or failure. While randomness is a core part of the roguelike genre, there are moments where poor shop offerings or early unit losses can cripple a run beyond recovery, long before the player realizes it. Additionally, the food mechanic, while thematically interesting, can feel like an artificial limiter on exploration. If not managed carefully, it can create frustrating bottlenecks that push players into overly cautious strategies, rather than rewarding risk-taking.

Another area where the game falters slightly is in accessibility and pacing. The onboarding experience can feel minimal, with little explanation of how to build effective synergies or use mutations strategically. This learning curve is part of the appeal for those who enjoy trial and error, but it can also deter newer players or those less familiar with auto-battlers. Moreover, the later stages of a run can feel repetitive once the initial excitement of discovery wears off, and some units or builds can feel noticeably stronger than others, suggesting balance is still a work in progress.

Still, for all its quirks and occasional frustrations, Despot’s Game succeeds in delivering a deeply entertaining and highly replayable strategy experience. It’s a game that encourages creativity through chaos and rewards players who embrace its offbeat world. With continued updates, an active community, and a developer clearly invested in expanding its systems and content, the game is steadily evolving into a cult favorite among roguelike and auto-battler fans. Its unique mix of humor, strategy, and unpredictability makes it a standout in a genre that often plays it safe, and it's well worth checking out for anyone looking for something truly different.

The rest of this review isn't about a con, so much as a warning. Something that will save you time if you decide to try it: 

It can be difficult to figure out what will/won't benefit your little band of puny humans in the long run. There's loads of different paths you can take with your very limited resources, and the wrong choice gets you killed. Do you put points into:
Mutations, which are buffs for your entire squad?
Shop Upgrades?
New Equipment, in order to get synergy bonuses?
More food?
More people?

Early on, I spent a few runs investing into what I thought was best, only to be stomped by the enemy as soon as I hit the first difficulty spike. That zombie level that the negative reviews are talking about? Yeah, that's the first spike. It's where the game punishes you for not investing into [spoiler]Mutations, which are by far the best long-term investment.[/spoiler] It's abrupt, and the first couple of times it can be infuriating. I don't blame anyone at all for noping out after losing 1,3,5+ times to the same level pretty early on. The key is to just read the tooltips on EVERYTHING and actually math out the buffs/debuffs. The game gives you what you need, but it's not always great about making sure you know that. 

Anyway, thanks for reading this far if you did. Give the game a shot. I think it deserves the praise it's gotten.

Despot's Game: Dystopian Army Builder is a roguelike strategy game.
 
[h1]A Run[/h1]
Consists of several levels. Each level consists of a handful of rooms while each room has an enemy in it, the reward varies from being able to buy food, to humans or having events in them. You can also get free mutants on altars or fight against bosses. Random events happen after every level and sometimes within them in special rooms.
 
[h1]Battles[/h1]
It's pretty easy actually. You have humans, either with a weapon attached or "naked". You can place them on the battlefield how you want. Click on "Fight" and the battle starts. From here on, it is like an auto-battler. Your humans will fight automatically and you can sit back and watch.
This means, the strategy comes from placing your humans accordingly, plan ahead when it comes to food, weapons, and mutations as well as how to approach which rooms. After every battle, you will get tokens. Tokens are your main currency to buy food, humans, mutations, and weapons with.
 
[h1]Humans[/h1]
They are your main resource. Each human needs one food for every move (One move means going into a room). If you don't have any food left, they will suffer from debuffs while worst case means, they will die. To save yourself, you can sacrifice one human for five pieces of food. Some rooms let you buy food for tokens, too.
Every human is naked, without any kind of weapon. You can buy different weapons in the shop and equip a human with them to improve their stats.
 
[h1]Classes[/h1]
There are dozens of classes available such as Shooter, Medic, Fighter, Tank, Cultist, and a lot more. Having several units one of class, each with a different weapon grants them special abilities like having three cultists will let them summon a tentacle and so on.
This also adds to the tactical depth of the game.
 
[h1]King Of The Hill[/h1]
This is the multiplayer "mode" of Despot's Game. When you Win a run, your party will be placed on the leaderboard. To determine your spot on the leaderboard, you will fight against other parties one after another. Winning means you will beat his spot and go up, losing will let you go down.
It's pretty thrilling even though you just sit back and watch it happen. Every other party is from another REAL player. This adds a lot of tension to the game.
 
[h1]Meta Progression[/h1]
There is nothing to make future runs easier really. Well, you will unlock the "easy" difficulty but since this mode deactivates your ability to be placed on the leaderboard (King Of The Hill), it's not really an option to fully enjoy the game. More so to try out stuff and learn the game more.
You will unlock starting builds, mutations to unlock in future runs, etc. while playing.
 
[h1]Differences between the Demo and Full Version[/h1]
Everyone who played the demo will have a pretty good feeling of what the game will be like. Two things changed compared to the full game: There is more of everything (Units, events, monsters, difficulties, mutations, etc.) AND the game got a lot harder. First of all, a run is longer now and the balance changed. Some things like food are more expensive, while some enemies got weaker, others got stronger, too.

[h1]The Good[/h1][list]
[*]It's addictive. While I'm not much of a fan of auto-battlers, I'm in love with Despot's Game. In fact, I think it's so addictive, this deserves to be on the list for the best Strategy Games of '21.
It's just so fun to plan ahead and watch your little humans fight.
[*]It's tactical demanding. There is a lot of strategies involved to win a run and be placed on the leaderboard. From placing your humans on the battlefield to asking yourself what I really need to buy right now or should I spare some tokens for later, or even new mutations?
[*]The balance between RNG and Skill. While it has some kind of RNG (What's available in the shop, which mutations you can get, etc.) it doesn't feel unfair. It's so well balanced, that RNG won't affect your run too much. I never had the feeling of me losing because I got bad luck rather me being dumb, not going for X, predicting something "wrong", etc.
[*]King of the Hill. I usually dislike leaderboard or at least don't care much for them but not in Despot's Game. It's just so much fun to be placed on the leaderboard.
[*]The writing is funny. While there isn't that much text, events are very humorous.[/list]
 
[h1]The Bad[/h1][list]
[*]While I think the demo was a bit too easy, I feel like they went a bit too hard on the full game. I won my third or fourth try in the demo (it was a pretty easy run) but after around four hours and dozens of tries, I wasn't even able to reach the final boss/stage. Maybe I just need more time to "get good" but maybe it's a bit too hard right now.
[*]Too few events. Already had some events repeated in my third run (not counting events from the demo of course).
[*]Minor bugs like sometimes mouse clicks don't register and some Units get stuck and don't attack for a few seconds.
[*]The music is monotonous and gets annoying fast.[/list]
 
[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Despot's Game: Dystopian Army Builder is one of the best strategy games in 2021. It's addictive, tactical demanding, humourous, innovative, and just fun. King of the Hill is a very nice addition to boring Leaderboards, it's difficult enough to be engaging and perfectly balances RNG and Skill IMO.
I can't get enough of the game and while I think it's a little bit too hard on normal, I can't say this is too bad as of now. Adding more events and different enemies would be a nice addition as well as fixing units getting stuck but aside from that, this is a well-crafted game. I'm excited to see what else they have in store for us during early access.
 
If you're into tactical roguelikes, you should definitely buy Despot's Game.

Are you a casual player who likes to beat singleplayer games with overwhelming power?

Are you a PvP-focused player who likes to theorycraft builds while precisely managing economy and randomized upgrades?

If yes to either, there's something here for you. Do be aware that the PvE portion of the game is quite easy to beat on most settings, but that's also not the point. Its easy if you maximize your current power, but there's incentives in place to handle the PvE as lightly as possible while you bank resources for a huge power spike late in the run. Because if you do, you'll be more competitive in the post-run asynchronous PvP.

Also, be aware there is a non-trivial unlock system that may put you at a disadvantage for awhile (~20 runs?), and a PvP bracket system that prevents newer players from being exposed to the top/active players until they do well in a few seasons worth of newer opponents. Realistically, this is good for most players, but if you're the hardcore competitive type, this means waiting potentially months before facing harsh competition.

Another reviewer put it best: the biggest problem this game has right now is that it's prone to death spirals.

If you come out of a particularly nasty battle, you'll find it impossible to recover. Lose 1-2 dudes? You'll probably be fine, though you'll struggle in the next few rooms due to your lower damage/healing/tankiness.

3-5 dudes die in a fight? You've now opened yourself for more people to die. And sure, you'll survive the next fights, but you'll take more losses along the way. Even if you run into a shop to buy more men and items, you won't be able to replace everyone. And the ones you do replace will be level 1 vs. the level 3-5's you lost, and may not be the items you lost.

Oh, and if you lose front line units, you've opened your back line up to tons of damage they can't tank. If you lose your back line, then your tanks have to take more damage before the enemies die, opening the possibility for more death.

Let's say you replace a back line unit. It'll be safe and chilling in the back line (with exceptions, depending on what floor you're on) and gain plenty of experience with ease.

Replace a front line unit? You better hope it never gets targeted because it won't survive if it does.

Lose over 5 units? Your team will meet a slow, agonizing death over the next 5 rooms if you're lucky. Between 3-5, you'll probably meet your end on the next floor at best.

The game tries to rectify this by having the default game mode have a chance for units to drop items when they die. THIS IS A GOOD SYSTEM, but it isn't enough.

Sadly, the solution to this problem is not simple, but I have full faith in the dev(s). They have something good going on. Now they have to work out what problems it's having because it's new. It's gonna be tricky, because balancing between making it easier but still hard as hell is difficult.

This game has other flaws, some of which will be worked out as it continues through Early Access. I can easily say though that this is a game to keep an eye on.

Nothing. The graphics are amazing (especially if you're into pixel art)!

TLDR: a somewhat shallow pve-centered autobattler with pvp at the end of a run. Great visuals, catchy music, sassy dialogue during events, which were a highlight of the game; decent variety of game modes and constant balance updates. Lacking in some qol and, if you go for 100% achievements, it overstays its welcome. Still would recommend DBS: it’s not groundbreaking, but well made.  Developers definitely care about the game.
What strikes right away is a very strong visual side of the game: the pixel art and animation quality is really high, with attention to small things – looks absolutely fantastic. The music is cool and catchy.
Most of playtime is pve with a boss at the end. It’s hard to fail a run, so, even though, most of the time is spent on building your team in pve, it’s all for the 2 mins or so of pvp at the end. The run usually takes, I’d say, about 40 to 60 minutes. Then you are paired against other players who have beaten the boss and, depending on the result of, usually 5-6 battles, you take a certain position in the rankings. It’s asynchronous: you don’t need to play at the same time. During subsequent runs, if you improve on your pvp part, your standings increase. Every 4 weeks or so there is a new season and generally, if you did all right, you move up the rank and repeat the cycle.
Your basic unit is a puny human whom you upgrade with items, which promote it to a certain class. Each class has 5 item tiers. By collecting several items with different tiers of a single class, you gain that class’ special ability. The variety comes from mutations, which you pick up as rewards: these come in form of passive bonuses, can give new abilities and synergies. During a normal run you easily acquire several dozens of mutations and these affect your build in a major way. In a sense, these are your build, and your team of humans is what actualizes it in game. You also have meta progression which affects only your current run.
Combat itself involves unit positioning: it matters (especially noticeable with smaller underpowered team) but the arrangement in the final build can be lenient as long as you put everyone where they generally should be. This was my first autobattler aside from small amount of hs: battlegrounds, so could be wrong on this one. 
Events are the highlight of the game. There are a lot of them: most occur at the beginning of a level and involve choosing options in dialogue that lead to different results. The writing and humor are great – enjoyed this part of the game very much. There are a dozen or so additional, level events which involve gameplay. These usually offer currency or an evolution, which is thematically connected to what an event was about. What I didn’t know for quite some time is that you can choose which level events you encounter: at levels 1,5 and 9  there is a lever in the wall. By pressing it you cycle through icons, each corresponding to a particular event. This way you can choose an event which is relevant to your build and not rely on rng. 
There are several game modes present: the standard 12-level run, but there is also a shorter, 7-level version: takes less time, but levels are more packed with stuff, so in the end it all more or less evens out. There are no food modes too. Food is a cost which you pay every time you move through a maze, 1 per unit, so balancing your upkeep with how big is your party becomes important. For achievement hunters: play with food as soon as you can: certain events proc only in food runs, otherwise you won’t be able to collect all mutations. There are pve only modes too, so technically you can ignore pvp part of the game, but imo that is the most fun aspect. Balancing is also made around pvp. There is also a mode, which closely resembles tft and autochess gameplay: you fight against other players every 3 encounters. The teams are smaller and much less powerful, so the dynamics is quite different from standard runs. I played just a few runs so don’t have too much to say about that.
Its fun exploring and discovering what works, which combinations are synergetic. Your best performing build during a season is what other players will fight against when they finish the run. This also allows you to prepare for certain players, whom you know you’ll eventually fight. Building counter strategies was the most fulfilling experience during my time with the game. I didn’t get to high rank, mostly because you are gated from doing it too fast (not a skill issue, trust me;) You can only move one rank per season at max.
Note about achievements: the bottleneck is killing wheelmen. These are rare and it’s easy to have 4 or 5 runs without seeing one. There is a trick which can cut your grind time substantially, of which I learned too late. Always pick and carry a button which restarts current floor, preferably two. Once you get a wheelman, using an item will allow you to kill another one (or more. I think I had just one run with 3, rarely 2). With even better luck you can go infinite: kill the boss before encountering a wheeler. If the boss happens to drop a restart item, pick it; go kill the wheeler and reset. You’ll spawn after the boss and will be able to pick a button again. Highly suggest taking advantage of this trick if you get it: the wheelers are THAT rare. 
Now for the criticism:
1)Despite many moving parts, there is not that much variety. It doesn’t take long to try all the classes and combos. Depending on the season, some builds are way stronger, which makes an amount of viable options even smaller. The strategy part of the game is not very deep. Not necessarily a negative, but I would like more depth.
2)I learned after 30+ hours that you can move with wasd. The first thing I do in any game I start is go to options, check those, and next – to controls. The game has a section with controls and shortcuts, but no wasd there, so I didn’t even consider trying that. Devs, PLEASE, inform me as a player of ALL hotkeys available in game.
3)There is no comprehensive in-game wiki. It shows all item tiers for respective classes but that’s all. So I can’t check the stats of units, I don’t know what class abilities do. Nowhere in game there is exact info on those. Sure, the game is rather casual, but it’s not that hard to include stats on all units and abilities. 
4)Your opponents’ builds in king of the hill (pvp part) are not saved anywhere. I don’t need infinite storage, but at least 5-10 of latest oppos’ builds should be saved, so I could check their mutations, meta and unit positioning. This can be solved by printscreening and then alt-tabing constantly while in-game and scrolling through couple dozen similarly looking screenshots. Not convenient at all.
5)Animations are great and I watch those for several runs, but then I want to skip through everything. There is an option to speed through events which very welcome and you can increase game speed; however it’s still WAY too slow. I’d say it’s marginally faster than what I would consider the base speed of the game should be. I’d prefer maybe x2 of current max speed. I would even use skip combat option, like in HoMM. Runs take too much unnecessary time. 
6)Some mutations are locked behind achievements, so I never used or encountered the wheeler one in game, because after the grind was over, I didn’t want to play anymore. Not enough variety or depth. The fix is simple: increase wheeler spawn rate or even make one guarantee to appear in any run.
Ultimately I would recommend the game. It has issues but the vibes are nice. I doubt many players will sink more than several dozen hours, but the time spent was fun. The writing, memes and references are great. Plus the game gets constant balance updates - developers definitely care. Good job!

In response to the complaints of the game being too hard or certain units being imbalanced, I don't think that's true. This is a game you have to first learn and until you do, you will likely die on a run. All of your decisions matter and if you move around or spend your money carelessly, your run will fail. Once you figure it out, finishing a run becomes trivial and the challenge becomes being as efficient as possible to maximize your team's effectiveness for the king of the hill pvp battle that comes after (king of the hill pits you against a leaderboard of other players who have finished a run).

This game likes to present you with gameplay taxes in the guise of gameplay mechanics. Difficulty is inflated by meaningless comedy dialogue exchanges which generally result in unpredictable penalties. Flexibility in building teams is mixed, as both the singular healer units and the singular tank units are obligatory picks due to the combination of zero sources of consistent healing, tiny unit health pools, and high enemy damage. Cross your fingers that you get the opportunity to fill your army with these units. DPS units are your only flexibility source, and they're largely interchangeable in effectiveness.

Above all, the food mechanic presents nothing of enjoyment and is perhaps the fastest tax clock I've ever encountered. Extremely frustrating as the game is a room-tile exploration type game, and if you somehow ended up at the wrong side of the grid from the boss, you are going to be taxed for every room backtracked.

The auto chess style is there, but held back by key factors. The food system discourages you from building up your strategy/army. The loss of items on unit death means you may have your synergies strangled in the crib, or your army crippled permanently after a hard battle. Before battle, you can see where enemies will be, but not what kind of unit they will be. This means there's little to no point in adjusting your formation, as you simply cannot strategize meaningfully against what you will face. Perhaps most importantly, the effects of stacking units in a class just aren't that interesting. Extremely simple base effects, with equally simple raw number increases.

The game is gorgeous and I like everything about the concept, but the experience just doesn't spark joy. I'm a roguelike player by far and above every other genre I play, I'm no stranger to randomization, rough starts, and playing by what the RNG graces me with. This game just doesn't give you enough to work with.

I have to agree with the other negative reviews here - While I like the general concept of the game, the difficulty and binary nature of winning or losing combats doesn't feel great. The lack of any real comeback mechanic can leave you effectively dead but forced to play through another four or five combats to finally die against the floor boss that you could never have beaten. One of the bigger issues here I think is the lack of meaningful boosts to your units outside of the mutations - something like armour or other individualised boosts you could put on key units to boost their survivability, or perhaps a mechanic to smush several units into one superunit (would be pretty on brand). 

The general balancing of the different classes also feels way off - healers seem to become pretty useless as the game goes on but practically essential early, and cultists/eggheads feel very bad and awkward to use - while mages and tricksters feel very overtuned at the start and scale very well into the later floors. Some of the enemies have a tendency to just decimate your frontlines and, if not outright end your run there cripple you in the aforementioned 'already dead but forced to keep playing' way - cerberus has ended three of my runs so far by effectively oneshotting my entire set of frontline units. 

Food is a mechanic that just feels like it has no place in the game.  You aren't rewarded for having plenty of food - just punished for not having enough, It's a resource that has the sole purpose of eating into your tokens 
 and I'd honestly rather just receive less tokens and not have to hassle with it. In a practical sense it places a cap on the number of units you can field at a given time, which doesn't feel too great as after a certain point MORE MEATSHIELDS is the only real strategy to get stronger.

The design ethos of the game seems a bit confused, in that it simultaneously tries to treat your units as expendable 'puny humans', while also making them quite hard to replace in a practical sense and providing you with various mutations (e.g 25% chance to revive) that only really make sense if you're fielding very large numbers of these units, which food heavily limits.

I rarely write negative reviews for games, but I really feel like I have to in this case. The game hits so many good marks, but somehow in all of it, ends up falling flat. To put it in simple terms; it's just not fun, not for me anyway.

I'll summarize my thoughts briefly, and go into more detail later:

Pros:
- Banging soundtrack. The music is easily one of the best aspects of the game.
- Good art. The art style is unique and very nice to look at.
- Simple mechanics. The complexity of the game lies in tactics, rather than convoluted systems.
- Witty writing. A lot of the quest dialogues are well written and feature nice references.

Cons:
- High difficulty. The game expects you to die a lot as you figure things out.
- Lack of comeback. If you're barely hanging on, there's very little to do but to run into the next encounter and die.
- Cumbersome. Food as a resource is just... annoying. It's not hard to manage and only serves to curb your power.
- Lack of variety. The game boasts several classes, all of which feel very same-y. Worst of all the units within those classes act essential the same.

I genuinely tried liking the game. My initial reaction was quite positive, there's a lot to love in this game. However, ultimately it just feels like a very "meh" experience, and I don't think it needs to be that way. 

Food should either go or be reworked, I genuinely find it adds nothing to the game. Whenever you add something to a game, a developer should ask themselves "Does this make the game more fun?" and if the answer is no, they just shouldn't add it. The game is about exploration, finding new areas, doing fetch quests... but then it punishes the player for doing so by arbitrarily limiting the amount you can explore. Worst of all, it's harder to explore the larger you army since it costs more food. If this would only apply to new locations, alright, I think that would be an improvement, but every single step you take costs food, and it can be extremely frustrating to walk into dead-ends because of it.

Healers are a big problem in my opinion. You need healers for a successful run, I've not had luck get anywhere far at all if I wasn't running healers because there's no automatic health regeneration. I understand the game's gimmick is all about replacing your pawns, but there's not an efficient way to do that, and the game's level-up system of individual units kind of runs exactly counter to that very philosophy. And if you have a class that's a "must-have" in every run, it simply begs the question "shouldn't this be a base functionality?"

Variety is cool to have, but the game really doesn't do a good job at portraying it. Most of the classes feel the same, what's the difference between a Thrower and Shooters? Attack Speed and a Bomb ability, on paper that's different, but in reality you wouldn't see much of it. I'm not sure if it's a lack of effects, but the bonuses just feel so... minor.

Maybe that's the keyword here. Everything increases your stats by such low and insignificant amounts it's just not satisfying. It feels like playing World of Warcraft back in the day, when you would level up just to get a new talent that gives you "2% extra damage". Now, maybe that changes further into the game, because eventually if you get enough bonuses they start to stack up, but I don't even get to the very late game stages because I'm so infuriated by the first couple floors.

All being said, the game's still in early access and I can see the devs are reworking things and adding new stuff. That's good, I think in time this game may turn out to be good. But for now, I genuinely am just not having a good time, though I wish I did.
