The frustrating thing about this game isn't that it's hard, but that the optimal strategy isn't very fun.

1. Upgrade your shop as soon as possible.
2. Build your first high level unit as soon as possible.
3. Don't build low level units.
4. Don't build a variety of units.
5. Focus all of your upgrades onto one or two unit types.
6. Win the game with only the highest level units of one or two types.

The problem extends to the food system. Don't get me wrong, I enjoy some resource management with my strategy. But once again, the optimal strategy (at the time of this review) is corny as hell. *Ignore food.* Yes, you heard me. Ignore it. Walk around with a food shortage for several turns, and when you're close to facing the consequences (I'm assuming there are consequences), THEN buy exactly one turn of food. You can now walk around for another several turns with a food shortage.

Is this the intended design? I don't know. I don't think so. I think the game assumes you'd want to keep enough food around at all times. But leaning into the shortage saves you a ton of tokens. The food economy is less "keep stocked up" and more "make sure you arrive at a food stop before your food timer runs out, to pay the smallest possible fee". (Personally, I think the game should just accept that food is broken, and change the mechanic to exactly that: find a rest stop every few turns.)

The question "is this actually the intended design?" goes back to the heart of the game. 

I want to like this game more than I did. And at the beginning, the game shows a lot of potential, as I experimented with the systems. The central question of the game seems compelling: "how do I combine my units in interesting and useful ways?" 

But the answer is you don't. And the fun quickly melted away when you learn that the secret to the game is to build just one unit, over and over, and funnel your upgrades into making them a powerhouse.

So why am I writing this review? It's because I believe this game has potential. And I wouldn't have spent so much time analyzing the game if I didn't think there was the seed of a good idea in here somewhere. 

The game vaguely reminds me of FTL – a much better game, but also a game that this could aspire to become. FTL has a bigger variety of strategies, based on combining different abilities instead of just focusing on one or two things. (Of course, there's also the fun of actually controlling those strategies, which this game leans against with its automation, but I can accept that.) 

I like to imagine a better version of Despot's Game where there are more interesting synergies than "pick two unit types and upgrade the hell out of them". But for now, this game isn't there yet.

Despot's Game is a nice little auto battler with beautiful graphics and fourth-wall breaking humor. I first played it when it was in early access and have come back to it a few times since then, but I do not enjoy it as much as I would like to, and I cannot recommend the game to everyone (at least not at full price).

In Despot's Game, you go through levels with random arrangements of rooms in typical roguelike fashion. Each level has a boss room which you need to find to proceed to the next level. Defeating the boss gives you the choice of one of two "buttons" (which two is determined randomly). These "buttons" (spells) can help you on the next floor (e.g. resurrect all units that died in the room you activate it, or heal all units for 30% of their health), but only before the fight, not during. Every room contains enemies and depending on the room, you will either be able to buy food, units & weapons, or choose a mutation (e.g. +x% attack speed) for your units after clearing the room. In this way, you can expand your army, where you are rewarded for combining units of the same class but with different weapons. As an example, the "Heal" ability of healers levels up with each additional healer you get that carries a different "weapon". This is a nice feature and the ability to restock the weapon shop for only two tokens (the game's currency) makes it possible to get some nice synergies after a few levels. Your units also level up automatically after defeating enemies, which rewards you for keeping them alive.
The currency is awarded for clearing rooms and can also be used for mutations, which are similar to a skill-tree.

However, expanding your army will require you to buy more food, as each unit going from one room to another uses up 1 food. This punishes backtracking and in combination with the random maps can feel very frustrating, as you are often forced to backtrack and/or may not find a room with food for quite some time. Some rooms allow you to teleport to other rooms with teleporters, but again, their random location on the map limits their use depending on the layout. I personally feel the teleporter rooms should allow one to teleport to any room one has discovered on the level.

After beating the final boss of the campaign, you can purchase units and weapons a final time, and the resulting army will then fight the armies of other people who beat the campaign. This is not very exciting, as your only interaction will be pressing the "Fight" button and waiting for your units to either win or lose the fight. The final ranking may reflect your skill to a certain extent, but quite likely it is also heavily influenced by how lucky you were during the run. Typically roguelikes only have leaderboards for a certain run which is identical for all users, but I am not sure if this is also the case here.

Overall I feel like the game has a lot of potential and is mostly fun, however the flawed food mechanic and the feeling that my army decisions have less impact than the path I choose on the map is what makes the game not worth my time at the moment.

[b]Overview[/b]

A game about herding human chaff through a meat processor run by a tyrant who’d be more compelling as a speeding ticket. The premise is Orwell's 1984 as written by a burnt out intern at a recently acquired mobile game studio. You’re told it’s a “dystopian battle simulator,” but really, it’s a spreadsheet where the cells scream when you delete them. 

The Despot is a non-entity, a void in a crown, a screensaver with delusions of grandeur. The “story” is a fortune cookie slip that says, “You’ll die confused.”

[b]Gameplay[/b]

You recruit units. They’re not characters, just placeholders with health bars. Assign them classes like “tank” or “wizard” or “healer,” titles as meaningful as “Assistant to the Regional Manager.” Feed them tokens scavenged from the digital gutter, mutate them with “upgrades” that might as well be a game of roulette. 

[i]“Your sniper just grew tentacles and now attacks by flinging his own teeth.”[/i]

Yeah, that’s real strategic depth.

Combat is a slot machine where the pitboss doesn’t even let you pull the lever. Position your units, hit “fight,” and watch the AI turn your genius plan into a house fire.

The RNG isn’t a mechanic — it’s the game laughing at you. Need a healer? Here’s a guy who heals enemies by accident. Need food? Here’s a “mystery meat” vendor winking at you like a sleazy used car salesman. 
The food system is a countdown clock to a foregone conclusion: You will fail, and the game will yawn.

Procedural generation is a con and a lazy excuse to recycle. The levels aren’t “generated” — they’re shuffled like a deck of cards someone spit on. You’ll see the same bleak corridors, the same boring altars where you trade a unit’s life for a +5% damage buff, and the same “special events.”Permadeath isn’t a consequence — it’s a shrug with a body count. Lose a unit? Replace them with another warm corpse. They’re all the same.

[b]Design[/b]

A Frankenstein’s monster of half-ideas and quarter-effort. Mutations are a coin toss where the prize is a live grenade. Some turn your squad into God, others brick your run because why not?

PvP is a joke, a spreadsheet duel against some kid’s sixth grade homework from three patches ago. Meta-progression is a stick with a carrot where the carrot is a new cosmetic for a unit.

The UI is an income tax return form. Tooltips explain nothing. Terms like “corruption” and “morale” are thrown around like confetti at a funeral. The tutorial is a loading screen that says “figure it out, dummy.” Learning the game isn’t an engaging journey — it’s a hostage situation.

[b]Aesthetic[/b]

It’s pixel art for people who think art is a screensaver. The visuals are a slurry of brown and gray, the color palette of a nihilist. The Despot’s dialogue is edge-lord gibberish, the “lore” is a sticky note that reads “humans = bad.” The soundtrack is synth-wave for people who think Blade Runner is a vibe, not a movie. It’s not music. Just a tired backdrop with a beat.

[b]Retention[/b]

Roguelikes need surprises. This one’s as surprising as a Monday. After five hours, you’ve seen it all: the same enemies, the same loot, the same altars where a unit sacrifice earns you a participation trophy. The PvP is a ghost town. The mutations recycle. The only progression left is your resignation.

[b]The Illusion of Choice[/b]

Every decision is a false god. Sacrifice a unit for a marginal stat boost or let it starve? Equip the “Flaming Toaster Sword” or the “Poison Stapler?” 

It doesn’t matter. None of it. The RNG is the puppet master and you’re the sock. The game isn’t a challenge. It’s rigged to be as lethargic as possible.

[b]Conclusion[/b]

Despot’s Game isn’t a game. It’s a vending machine that eats money and dispenses yesterday's trash. A rogue-like for masochists who think a great day is a spreadsheet error. The mutations are pretty distractions, the combat a dice roll, the story is an idea on a used tissue. It’s not art. It’s not even a product. It’s the sound of a developer resigning to a life of decadence.

Overall, it’s a functional toaster if the toast was made of asbestos. You’ll play it, but only because you’ve already paid.

This game combines the genres of roguelike and autobattler to surprising effect, making something that's fun to boot up, play, and walk away from whenever you've had enough. The mutation system adds an additional layer of depth beyond just upgrading units, and it can be pretty tough to choose between buying items and buying team-wide upgrades. The soundtrack is also VERY good.

Currently, the game has a ton of potential, but feels unnecessarily punishing. The food mechanic leaves you completely at the mercy of map generation, as you don't know where the boss is until you're in an adjacent room, and your units require food every time you walk through a door. Please Konfa, remove the food cost for entering previously-explored rooms.

There's also the issue with transparency in the game's mechanics. There's no clear distinction between "damage" and "magic damage", and it's impossible to tell when your units are taking one type over the other.

You can pause the game and look at enemy abilities, but the only way you can really play around them is with unit positioning. There's an enemy that can teleport to the backline and one-shot all of your ranged units at once, and I still don't know how I'm expected to defend against it. Healers will also run into melee and die, even when you have the perk that allows them to heal from range.

The level of your units is incredibly important, making it vital to keep them alive at all costs... but there's absolutely no way to heal them outside of combat. All you can do is glare at your almost-dead tank while six medics wiggle around uselessly nearby, knowing that he's going to be one-shot in the next fight no matter where you move him.

The mutation upgrade tree is also a confusing mess, where you have to waste large amounts of money on stuff you don't even want. The perk that increases magic damage requires you to purchase SIX other upgrades first, and half of those don't have ANYTHING to do with magic damage builds, making them an unnecessary token sink. Want to upgrade the damage of summoned monsters? You have to upgrade your non-summoned units' armor first. This feels really bad in a game where the only real agency you have is with how you spend your money.

This game has a lot to offer even now, and I think most people can find fun in it, but I think it has a pretty long way to go.

Everything that you control is based around one resource. In reality, the balancing act is knowing how small to keep your army so that you can maximise upgrades until you get near the end and you inflate it quickly.

A lot of the upgrades are the same across unit types, so the more unique upgrades feel few and far between, and those upgrades are what let you play around with builds more, and upgrades aren't very common. Without the more unique upgrades you are more restricted to how you build your army, since there's only one real form of consistent healing and there's only one real form of consistent tank.

1.Class stacking/level cap: i dont hate the whole "have x different types of unit for a buff" as an idea, but in the late game it takes a goofy turn with levels being capped at 5 so the lower teir tank you have had for longer will always be worse then a higher tier one, but you cant get rid of them because you lose the class buff and you become stuck with it, some classes have less of this problem like cultists because you can have any amount and you get more benefit but most classes seem to hit a point where spamming higher tier units and ignoring the class buff works out best for raw power.

2. 3. Paid Mutations: if the currency is shared between shop/food/mutations thats not necessarily a problem, but i cant help but feel that the purchased mutations might be better as something placed in a shop, a lot of people complain about RNG here but i noticed after a while you start to pick out which mutations are the best to buy and every run starts to blend together a bit in doing so, its not a huge deal but it takes away some of the excitement of finding what your looking for.

5. Overall i had fun with the game when i first played it, came back after a few months to see how it looked after a bunch of updates and while it isnt bad i cant say id be itching to tell someone to play it, its funny, it looks good, but it lacks replay-ability outside of trying to complete challenges. My main gripes are with the gameplay flow where I'm either incredibly strong and snowball out of control. 
Or it's a negative death spiral where losing 1-2 units or not playing perfectly becomes a slow death.

I would rather die quickly than play out a dead run but I have to play out dead runs for a lot of the unlocks or the rare hope a mutagen saves me.

Compared to other autobattlers like tft, dota, and even the sad underlords there's less variety for units. It's also extra problematic as no unit seems to be individually different. all tanks tank. they don't have unique abilties and you're forced to keep them on for the set bonus upgrades. 

This is feature or lack of features makes the death spiral more prevalent since you're forced to keep lv1 shielders or boxing glove man in the back or they will die. When they die you will search for them via reroll for 1-2 tokens eating more at the tokens that will be used for more units or food costs. 

At this point, I should mention food, it's a fairly miserable mechanic to balance players from purchasing large armies to end the game quickly with capital. In practice, it just stops players from exploring more area and pushes them to seek lower/new levels faster since the rewards are greater. 

Because of the food mechanic players will look for mutagen rooms, food, and boss rooms. every other room is a skip or a minor bonus to make your party slightly better. You often don't need or even want to buy more units because of food or because you're already strong with the units you have. The tokens go to global tech tree improvements which often is the better investment. 

The event rooms which are a break from the heavy heavy combat play are often just a net loss of resources. 30 tokens or an incredibly niche mutagen. If the tokens scaled at all to which room i was in that might be nice. the 2nd floor event gives 30 and the 3rd or fourth floor event also gives 30? My fights per room nearly give that amount. 

The food mechanic actively hurts investigating these events. 

I'm frankly very disappointed that almost all the battles are just stat checks and positioning does not matter. If i'm strong enough i can position all my healers in the front and just let them spam heals since the ai is so terrible anyways it's sometimes been more effective especially with fighter teams. 

In conclusion, it's okay for what it is (flawed and fun) and it's in development but i still have several questions: Have the developers played other autobattler games? And if they did why did they take out the most interesting parts such as multiple item combinations, unique unit types, and even terrain based positioning for sets like tft's second season. 

In some cases I can see arguments for going wide means having less impactful and quality units but not every item in those other tft games were damage but they might have been for utility such as blink daggers etc that greatly improve the strategy. This game desperately needs more tactical choices for positioning and better AI or behaviors we can set.

This game insists upon itself while not being mechanistically sound. It looks good, but it is not a good game, and it fails to do the things, or hides them, what would make it rewarding. It has a lot of concepts that make a good game, but it's like the developer sometimes fails to see what these do for a game on a deeper level. And frankly I don't see the game getting better without redoing much of it's core concepts.

Examples:
-Food is too important in this game and punishes exploration which normally would be an important driving force. I get how this is an important balancing mechanism, but especcially on the later floors backtracking becomes a pain in the ass, while at the same time being pretty essential for the missions they offer.
-The missions offer very meh rewards for the PITA they are.
-The relics you collect have too little impact and many of them have unrewarding or unuseable effects. Some of them are an outright debuff even, or cancel eachother out. 
-The the boss rewards are meh.
-Playing conservative is the way to go for end-game, but very punishing in the beginning and highly RNG dependant.
-Playing with lots of food and guys always get you to midgame, but generally not further.
-In general there are to many brickwalls or skillchecks that just pop up. Many runs get shanked by completely random encounters that just stop your run that went perfect up to then.
-Team health management is lacking in possibilities.
-Many interactions between and properties of the many classes are unclear. A healer for instance, you'd think it would heal well, but quite often I just see them punch enemies and dying in the process while there are puppets to heal around them.
-Especcially late-game becomes a chaos of a lot of puppets flapping around, dying, and no real feedback on why or how.
-Almost all classes are glass cannons.
-Classes are not designed well around their role, the tanks are bad tanks, the healers don't heal enough, the shooters don't take cover, the evaders don't evade enough. The scientists and throwers are just random, unless you build the scientists in a specific (RNG) way. The cultists are designed well but it is weird how they go from a purely magic ranged type to a fully melee tank suddenly.
-It lacks visual feedback, the higer level skills classes get at a certain groupsize should be highlighted much better and have more effect.
-There is no meta-progresion and unlockables. Besides a few extra and unrewarding choices at the start. A run ends and then you pretty much only have the choice to do it again with marginally tweaked early game features, or upped difficulty that's just that, harder, but not more rewarding or diverse. Being able to skill into classes or puppet types, or starting loadouts or bonusses would really mae it more rewarding to replay.
-It lacks builds, or build potential. There are some good combinations of classes, which are just that; better than the rest purely from a power/survival standpoint. But not because they interact clearly or rewardingly. The relics and shop are so RNG that really working towards something only starts midgame. And even then, it's just getting a setup going and hope it survives the randomness.

Well, the idea is nice, but the autobattler part is done very poorly. Units are just stat sticks, with higher tier units having bigger stats, so while you do need different units of the same class to unlock bonuses, mostly you want all high tier units with exactly enough low tier to unlock to bonus. The main focus apparently is the random mutations you get during the run, but they are so random and have no identity (as every unit type can get every type of possible mutation, but the mutation is then tied to only that unit type) it's kinda not that interesting to work with them and mostly it's very basic stuff like, get good abilities for class X, try and get more of class X.
There's also the thing with food. Your guys "need" food or else they do less damage. However the actual correct way to play is starve your people a lot to save money to buy other stuff and only feed them occasionally, since eating once puts them back at full strength immediately. So while the game tells you to get your people food and even has the nice yellow and red warning bars, it's actually the wrong play and will just make you waste more time trying to beat it than necessary. A whole mechanic just there to be nothing more than a noob trap with no much else to go for.
Also the passive mutations you can buy at any time are nothing more than stats increases for the most part, making them also fairly boring among the sea of units that are themselves just stat sticks.

The thing at the end is kinda cool where you get to fight against other winning players teams, but really, the whole gameplay loop is fairly bland and the only thing that's gonna make people take so long to beat is all the noob traps set by the devs to make people chase the wrong direction imo.

Ever jumped in a pool shallow enough you hurt your legs?
Well, playing [b]Despot’s Game[/b] is the game equivalent of that.

[h1]X-Factor[/h1]
The hook of this title are the many animations and enemies the trailer portrays, and the chaos that ensues pitting your little army against the various monsters.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
Guide your stragglers room to room to autobattle, get credits to either buy equipment at the shop, food to stave off a hunger mechanic, or upgrades that will affect all characters in the party.

Rinse and repeat for 12 levels and you have this game.

There’s also a hunger mechanic where every time you move from room to room it will deplete a resource, giving you maluses and even a game over if you run dry of food, incentivizing you to build tall, to create through upgrades and gear an elite team of characters, instead of wide.

Another mechanic and maybe the most eyebrow-raising one, is to have many characters each with a different weapon, but in the same weapon category, despite each one being a straight upgrade to the others, in order to unlock/power up, the single class skill for the character.

[h1]Story[/h1]
There is none, Despot is a bored ai overlord that grows jelly-humans in a tube and gets pissy when they beat him at his own game, there’s not much else to it.

[h1]Downsides[/h1]
And here’s the big part of the review:

I expected there to be either more focus on customization, other than a single skill and a few modifiers given by RNG, and more to tactics as both your army and the enemy will just make a beeline to the closest target and autoattack it until it dies.

There’s little to no planning, since the best skills are locked behind RNG drops, and the skills you do have range from the very original “more health” and culminate with the just as original “more attack”.

The hunger mechanic feels tacked on, but fortunately there’s a way to turn it off.

The humor was also something that bogged down the experience, at least for me, and this is purely subjective.
Maybe you like a game where every character is a ADHD kid whose humor could be described by “lol so random, raise your sporks” and “Facebook memes”.

But the biggest problem is how barren the game feels, 

I don’t know how the dev made it... the game feels at the same time barren and “overcrowded”.
Barren because every weapon act the same, there’s just a stat change between them, besides a few having extra abilities to them, and each run being the same set of enemies, locations and bosses.
And overcrowded because with the many mechanics that introduces: Hunger, Multi same-class characters, feels like there’s a precise way to play, and you are just there rolling dices and following exactly the path that the game makes very clear you have to walk if you want a winning run.

Editing for clarity in response to the developer being kind enough to reach out: 

Let's assume you win every single run of this game that you play. You never lose, you always make it to KotH. 

First run of the game: You're learning the game and figuring out cool combos and unlocking mutations. You squeak out a win to KotH and woah, you snagged two victories. Great! 2/100.

You do it again, with newfound confidence and stronger mutagens and a more efficient strategy. You make it to the end, but your build wasn't meta, so you still squeaked out only 2 wins. 4/100. 

You try the meta build that you saw everyone else in KotH running. This time you racked up a cool 5 wins! 9/100. 

But running meta gets old after the third time in a singular season so you stop at 19/100.

You wait for a new season, and you come back only to find the balance is completely different and the game has been essentially upended from the previous meta. Rinse and repeat above approximately 6 times in total to receive your 100 wins. Each run, in my experience, takes close to 45 minutes to an hour. Let's just say 45 minutes consistently for simple math. 5 runs a season across 6 seasons to reach 100 wins in total, for 30 total runs at 45 minutes totaling 1350 minutes or about 23 hours. That's a decent time. 

Here's the thing: No one is consistently winning every run. Yeah ok there's mr pro gamer who does it, 1 guy out of thousands. The game has to not only balance PvP but also PvE. There are certain monsters that just rip your team instantly (lookin' at you dual cerberus) if you don't have just the right composition, or just the right mutations, or just the right levels.  It's the nature of a rogue-like to have RNG and require different builds and different parameters based on the situation. But when you try to mix it up and add some variety to your runs because it's boring running fencer, healer, gunner every single run for a victory, you're punished for it. Have you seen the state throwers are in? Whatever starting group has the thrower and shielder, it's instant death if you don't end up in a shop on your first node. If you have to do more than a singular battle, you instantly die. No exceptions. Where's the fun in that? 

The main problem is, your average player ends up getting no more than 10 wins in a season because this game just sucks to play after you win one or two runs. There's no wiggle room for variety in how you play the PvE aspect because some classes just blatantly suck or offer no start at all. And then when you get to PvP, as far as I'm aware the meta is still horde all the weapons for your desired build until you win using the usual cookie cutter builds to get there, then spam your units out for your desired build. I just don't find that fun.

KotH should've been a thing where the team that beats the final boss, whoevers left alive, jumps straight in, no prep time or jerry-rigging your teams into a meta. Instead, it's this weird meta-verse where you snake a few wins with a specific build that's unfun to run more than twice. 

Hopefully this explanation helps you understand why I hold an issue with 100 wins in KotH. At maximum, it's 100 runs won where you eek out 1 victory in KotH after. In reality, it's probably something like 40 victories where you average 3 wins after PvE. But that's not counting all the failed runs you'll do because you lost do to a mistake or bad RNG or you didn't find the one mutation that would seal your victory. (Note: Losing due to RNG or not finding the piece of the puzzle is not what makes this bad.)  I don't want to run the same Meta build every single time. That's boring. The premise of the game and the functional mechanics of the game are lovely. But the balance is atrocious, and the layout of how you get from point A to point B is incredibly stale. You can't run half the classes as a serious build because they're just bad. 

------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Win 100 KotH battles is an insane ask. Be reasonable.

TLDR: If you don't care about PvP, or if you do care about PvP but don't mind min-maxing via numerous restarts of your runs, then I'd recommend this game.

Ok hear me out.. it's easy to see the developer truly loves this game and dedicates their time to making it better. I hate leaving a "thumbs down" review on games that have a caring developer or dev team.
My review is coming from my personal experience with the game, not from whether or not you should buy it.

I think the game is a great idea, I like the classes, and roguelikes are my favorite genre.
If you remove "King of the Hill" from my experience, this game would get a thumbs up I think. KotH is the PvP mode you can play at the end of a PvE run. Whatever units you have at the end of the PvE run, and whatever upgrades you have, are what you take into PvP.
PvE isn't hard once you know how to play. My frustration is with PvP.

If you want to win PvP (place top 3, or especially finish a season in 1st place) you HAVE to min-max from the very very beginning of the PvE run (you have to restart over and over until you get the ideal augments). And there's typically only 1-2 comps that can place and hold top 3. You need to play them if you want top 3.
Once you know the comps that can place and hold top 3, you then have to get lucky in the PvE run and get all the perfect augments you need for your comp. It's also important to get the class-specific random events in PvE, that give your specific comp's class type a buff, and you need to win the random event, and then receive the correct reward.

I've played enough to finish 1st in a couple PvP seasons, and I've completed a PvE run in hardmode; I'm not just some frustrated new player. I feel like I have a strong grasp on mechanics and how to play.
I know roguelikes are "luck"-based. It's just... the amount of sub-par runs greatly outweighs good runs for me (bad or good being determined by upgrade choices and events/encounters).

It's honestly a very cool rougelike. To play a game is to engage with a bunch of random encounters, which can either kill you or give you some new "dice to roll" for the next encounter, and you get some ways to nudge the outcome in your favor. 

Designing this kind of game is to balance the lethality with the probability that a playthrough will yield a nice pile of dice rolls. If the game is too lethal, the player never feels like they can win. If the game gives away too much stuff, the feeling of reward for getting the stuff feels lame.

The reason I can't recommend this game is that it comes very close to nailing this but fails on the side of lethality. After playing a bunch of times I don't feel like it's reasonable for me to consistently get past a certain point in the game. The difficulty ramps up too sharply level by level, the "tokens" you get for victory is too little for you to build up an advantage, and the strategic paths available don't feel like good bets.

An auto-battler where you pick equipment, move from room to room in order to fight the end-boss and eventually 'other' players. I say 'other' because there's no way to verify that these players actually built said armies but we'll just assume the developers aren't trying to pull one over on us.

There are several game modes, some do not have this PVP element and some get you there quicker.  

Unfortunately, even though there is some method to the madness, it all feels a bit pointless as it is incredibly difficult or even impossible to estimate the effectiveness of something you've just done. And that 'other' player that just crushed you? Hopefully you were able to tell what the most effective unit was on his team because most of the time it's just a wall of humans facing another wall of humans. There's no way to rewind (Why not?) and trying to click on a unit to see some stats is often not possible with everything that's going on.

There's no real point in not completely filling up your part of the playing field with humans unless you're playing with the food mechanic on (which I suggest you disable unless you enjoy having even less control over decision making) and even then, you'll probably want to keep them all on for the PVP.

The statistics at the end don't mean much to me and I constantly have the feeling that although I enjoy auto-battlers, I don't particularly enjoy the poorly written and uninformative tool-tips (Try figuring out what magic damage is, for instance) and I constantly have the idea I should do something more productive, something that actually allows me to use my intelligence to crunch some numbers rather than just constantly guess. 

I'm sure there's whole websites dedicated to telling you exactly what the most effective build is and hopefully the RNG will get you there but I prefer figuring things out on my own and DG doesn't allow me to do that in a fun and time-efficient manner. Not recommend.
